records.sourceFile: How Humans Run Faster - The Neuromechanical Contributions of Functional Muscle Groups to Running at Different Speeds.pdf

paper.citation: Willer J, Allen SJ, Burden RJ, Folland JP. How Humans Run Faster: The Neuromechanical Contributions of Functional Muscle Groups to Running at Different Speeds. Scand J Med Sci Sports. 2024;34(8):e14690.
paper.abstract: Eleven male middle-distance runners ran on an instrumented treadmill at six speeds from 2.78 to 8.33 m/s. Inverse dynamics quantified the positive and negative work of flexor and extensor moments for each functional muscle group, and EMG was recorded from eight muscles per leg. Ankle plantar flexors were the largest stance-phase contributor at all speeds. Hip extensors and knee flexors became the dominant whole-stride contributors at higher speeds.
paper.tldr: At higher running speeds, hip extensors and knee flexors carry most of the stride's work, while plantar flexors remain the main contributors during stance. Plantar flexor stance kinetics track step length, and hip extensor swing kinetics track step frequency.
paper.methods: Eleven male middle-distance runners ran at six treadmill speeds with kinematics, ground reaction forces and surface EMG from eight muscles per leg. Joint moments and the positive and negative work of flexor and extensor moments were summed by functional muscle group. Linear mixed-effect models related kinetic variables to step length and step frequency.
paper.findings: Ankle plantar flexors contributed more than 60% of stance positive and negative work at all speeds, but their share of whole-stride work declined with speed. Hip extensors became the largest whole-stride positive-work contributor above 5 m/s, and knee flexors became the largest whole-stride absorber above 7.22 m/s. Plantar flexor peak moment and positive stance work explained 97% and 96% of the variance in step length. Hip extensor peak moment and positive swing work explained 98% and 99% of the variance in step frequency.
paper.limitations: The sample was 11 men with a relatively homogeneous middle-distance profile, and the top speed was below elite sprint speed. Net joint moments may understate muscle group forces because of co-contraction. EMG was limited to eight muscles, and some sample sizes were reduced to n = 7. The across-speed correlations do not show that changing plantar flexor kinetics would change step length.
paper.practicalImplications: Coaches can use the finding that plantar flexors carry most stance work at all speeds, while hip extensors and knee flexors carry most whole-stride work at high speeds, to set conditioning priorities. The associations come from one treadmill protocol, so they should guide, not dictate, training choices.
paper.athleteDev: Plan conditioning around the muscle groups that carry the most work at the speeds an athlete trains. Plantar flexor capacity may matter most for lower-speed running, and hip extensor and knee flexor capacity for high-speed running.
paper.rtp: This study of healthy runners on a treadmill cannot guide return to sport after injury. It does not show that any muscle group is weak or injured, so it cannot set return-to-run criteria.

records.sourceFile: Human foot muscle strength and its association with sprint acceleration, cutting and jumping performance, and kinetics in high-level athletes.pdf

paper.citation: Tourillon R, Michel A, Fourchet F, Edouard P, Morin JB. Human foot muscle strength and its association with sprint acceleration, cutting and jumping performance, and kinetics in high-level athletes. J Sports Sci. 2024.
paper.abstract: In 52 high-level athletes, the authors tested the association between maximal MTP flexion torque and sprint acceleration, cutting and jumping performance and ground reaction force kinetics, and whether adding other foot and leg variables improved the models. MTP torque was moderately associated with maximal-speed sprint kinetics, where models including MTP torque explained 28% and 35% of variance, while acceleration and cutting performance were explained mainly by plantarflexor and quadriceps strength.
paper.tldr: In this group of injury-free athletes, forefoot (MTP) flexion strength was moderately linked to maximal-speed sprint kinetics and to 10 m time in the high-acceleration condition. It was not linked to cutting or vertical jump performance, and higher gripping strength went with lower horizontal jump power, so its training value is untested.
paper.methods: Cross-sectional study of 52 injury-free athletes (47 men, 5 women) at national level in five sports. MTP flexion torque was measured with a custom dynamometer, and sprint acceleration, 90-degree cutting, vertical and horizontal countermovement jumps and foot-ankle hops were recorded on force platforms with timing gates. Pearson correlations and stepwise backward multiple regressions were used, with foot posture, foot deformation, ankle plantarflexor and quadriceps torque, and reactive strength added to the models.
paper.findings: Relative MTP pushing and total torque were moderately associated with 10 m sprint time in the high-acceleration condition (r = -0.33, p = 0.02) and with relative effective vertical impulse (r = 0.42, p = 0.03) and contact time (r = -0.41, p = 0.04) at maximal speed. Higher gripping torque was associated with lower horizontal jump peak power (r = -0.35, p = 0.01), and no MTP torque variable was associated with vertical jump height or cutting time. Models combining MTP torque with foot deformation or foot-ankle reactive strength explained 28% and 35% of variance in maximal-speed impulse and contact time; acceleration (27% to 36%) and cutting (35%) models did not retain MTP torque, and jump models (26% to 38%) retained only gripping torque, for horizontal power.
paper.limitations: The design is cross-sectional and correlational, so causal effects cannot be inferred. Strength was measured at one joint angle only, the hip was not measured, and the sample was young (mean age 20.1 years), 90% male and from five sports. The sample size was calculated for an assumed r of 0.70, which no observed correlation reached, so the authors note possible underpowering. Sprint data came from several trials with different starting points. The Discussion gives 37% of variance for contact time, while the Results give an adjusted r2 of 0.35. The explained variance comes from models that include other variables, not from MTP torque alone, and the Discussion attributes 23% and 26% of vertical jump variance to quadriceps torque and foot flexibility, while the Results report 26% to 38% for jump models.
paper.practicalImplications: Forefoot (MTP) flexion strength can be considered as one part of a profile when assessing sprint and jump capacity, mainly for maximal-speed sprint kinetics. The authors suggest adding MTP flexion and foot-ankle reactive strength exercises to development programmes, but this study did not test training, so treat it as a hypothesis to trial and measure. Keep ankle plantarflexor and quadriceps strength in view: together they explained acceleration performance, plantarflexor torque contributed to cutting, and quadriceps torque contributed to jumping.
paper.athleteDev: Consider testing forefoot flexion strength as part of a performance profile for sprinters and field athletes. The study links it to maximal-speed sprint kinetics, but not to cutting or vertical jump height. Pair any forefoot work with reactive strength and plantarflexor strength, and track changes in sprint outcomes to test whether the link holds in your athletes.
paper.rtp: The sample was injury-free and the study did not assess return to sport or rehabilitation. It cannot inform return-to-play decisions or set strength targets for injured athletes.

records.sourceFile: Hypoxia and resistance exercise - a comparison of     localized and systemic methods.pdf

paper.citation: Scott BR, Slattery KM, Sculley DV, Dascombe BJ. Hypoxia and Resistance Exercise: A Comparison of Localized and Systemic Methods. Sports Medicine. 2014;44:1037-1054.
paper.abstract: Narrative review of resistance exercise under localized hypoxia (blood flow restriction, BFR) and systemic hypoxia (intermittent hypoxic resistance training, IHRT). The authors summarize adaptive, perceptual and mechanistic evidence for each method and compare their practical limits. They suggest IHRT may suit athletic populations but state that few studies allow firm recommendations.
paper.tldr: Low-intensity BFR training can build muscle and strength more than the same training without BFR, but its mechanisms are not settled. Resistance training in systemic hypoxia looks promising for athletes, but the evidence is thin.
paper.methods: Narrative review, with no described search method, of published studies on resistance exercise with BFR and with systemic hypoxia. It covers morphological, strength, perceptual, hormonal, metabolic and signalling responses. Tables 2 and 3 summarize acute and training studies of systemic hypoxia.
paper.findings: BFR studies report larger gains in muscle cross-sectional area and strength after low-intensity training (about 20 to 50 percent 1RM) than the same training without BFR, with inconsistent responses for IGF-1, testosterone and myostatin. For systemic hypoxia, the review cites a 5-week study in netball athletes in which both IHRT and BFR gave greater strength and muscle size gains than normoxic training, and a 4-week study with no advantage for hypoxia.
paper.limitations: The review does not describe how studies were selected or how evidence quality was judged. The authors note that IHRT research is limited, that the mechanisms remain poorly understood, and that low-intensity BFR does not produce the same motor unit activation as high-intensity training taken to failure.
paper.practicalImplications: BFR may suit people who cannot tolerate moderate or high loads, such as older adults, rehabilitation patients, or athletes managing total training load. The authors suggest IHRT may suit athletes because multi-joint lifts can be trained at higher intensity, but they say current understanding does not allow firm recommendations. Cuffs must be applied with experience, since inappropriate use can cause petechiae, numbness and dizziness.
paper.athleteDev: Low-intensity BFR can add a muscle and strength stimulus when heavy loads are not suitable, for example when managing total training load. Resistance training in systemic hypoxia may suit athletes because multi-joint lifts can be trained at higher intensity, but the review says the evidence is too thin for firm training recommendations.
paper.rtp: The review mentions rehabilitation patients as a possible BFR population and proposes that BFR could reduce joint stress, but it does not test return-to-sport outcomes or injury rates. It cannot set return-to-sport loading or clearance criteria.

records.sourceFile: Impact of Blood Flow Restriction                                Exercise on Muscle Fatigue Development and            Recovery.pdf

paper.citation: Husmann F, Mittlmeier T, Bruhn S, Zschorlich V, Behrens M. Impact of Blood Flow Restriction Exercise on Muscle Fatigue Development and Recovery. Med Sci Sports Exerc. 2018;50(3):436-446.
paper.abstract: Laboratory study of 17 resistance-trained, physically active males comparing four sets of low-intensity knee extension with and without blood flow restriction. The authors tracked maximal voluntary torque, electrically evoked twitch torque and voluntary activation during and after exercise. BFR produced faster and larger fatigue during exercise, and the effect diminished within about 2 minutes of reperfusion.
paper.tldr: Low-intensity knee extension with blood flow restriction causes more muscle fatigue than the same work without restriction, mainly through reduced contractile torque. The extra loss of maximal torque was gone within 2 minutes of cuff release, although some twitch-torque differences persisted longer.
paper.methods: Within-subject, randomized, counterbalanced design with two sessions. Participants did four sets (30, 15, 15 and 15 repetitions at 30 percent 1RM) with BFR at 60 percent of arterial occlusion pressure, or without BFR. Neuromuscular tests (MVC, interpolated twitch, paired stimuli at 10 and 100 Hz, single stimuli) were done before, after each set, and at 1, 2, 4 and 8 minutes of recovery, with EMG, RPE and leg pain recorded.
paper.findings: After the first set, BFR caused larger reductions in MVT, PS100 twitch torque and the PS10:PS100 ratio than control. At exercise termination, MVT fell 44.5 percent with BFR and 24.3 percent in control, and voluntary activation fell more with BFR (10.2 vs 3.2 percent). Twitch torque recovered substantially within 2 minutes after BFR, while voluntary activation was reduced in both conditions at 1 minute and MVT had not fully recovered by 8 minutes.
paper.limitations: Only men were tested and the sample was small, so sex differences in fatigability are not addressed. Peripheral nerve stimulation cannot show whether spinal or supraspinal factors caused the impairment in neural drive, and the authors infer group III/IV afferent mechanisms without measuring them.
paper.practicalImplications: Low-intensity BFR produces large fatigue within a session, so set loads and rest periods with that in mind. The authors suggest low-intensity BFR may suit high-frequency hypertrophy training because much of the torque loss recovers within minutes of cuff release, but this single-session study tested no training outcomes and MVT was still about 13 percent down at 8 minutes.
paper.athleteDev: Within a session, low-load BFR produced large early torque loss and higher perceived effort, so set loading should account for that. The authors propose low-intensity BFR for high-frequency hypertrophy work, but the study measured acute fatigue only, not performance or adaptation.
paper.rtp: The study measured acute fatigue in healthy men and did not include injured people or return-to-sport tests. It cannot show whether BFR work is safe after injury or set loading for return to sport.

records.sourceFile: Impact of hip flexion angle on unilateral and bilateral Nordic hamstring exercise torque and high density electromyography activity.pdf

paper.citation: Hegyi A, Lahti J, Giacomo JP, Gerus P, Cronin NJ, Morin JB. Impact of Hip Flexion Angle on Unilateral and Bilateral Nordic Hamstring Exercise Torque and High-Density Electromyography Activity. Journal of Orthopaedic & Sports Physical Therapy. 2019;49(8):584-592.
paper.abstract: This laboratory study compared knee flexion torque and high-density EMG of the BFLH and ST during bilateral and unilateral Nordic hamstring exercise performed with neutral hips and with 90-degree hip flexion. Thirteen amateur football and rugby players completed the four exercise variants at an eccentric 1-repetition maximum load. Hip flexion to 90 degrees produced higher torque and lower EMG in both muscles.
paper.tldr: Hip position changes how the Nordic hamstring exercise loads the hamstrings. Flexing the hips to 90 degrees gave more knee flexion torque with less muscle activity, while neutral hips gave more activity, especially in the BFLH near full knee extension.
paper.methods: Thirteen amateur football and rugby players performed bilateral and unilateral Nordic hamstring exercise with neutral hips (NHE0) and with 90-degree hip flexion (NHE90) at an eccentric 1-repetition maximum load, with knee motion paced at about 15 degrees per second. Torque came from a load-cell device, and 15-channel high-density EMG was recorded from each of the BFLH and ST. Curves were compared with statistical parametric mapping.
paper.findings: NHE90 produced higher knee flexion torque than NHE0 across most of the movement in the bilateral mode (0% to 87%) and throughout the unilateral movement. Both BFLH and ST were more active in NHE0 than in NHE90, and bilateral and unilateral modes gave similar peak torque and EMG when load was matched. Bilateral NHE0 produced higher torque than unilateral NHE0 only in the midrange (52% to 78%).
paper.limitations: The sample was small (13 amateur male players), and the authors state that this may have raised the false-negative rate and biased the effect sizes. Surface EMG is prone to cross-talk, knee angle came from the device potentiometer rather than direct measurement, and torque and EMG were recorded from the dominant leg only. One author is the inventor and patent owner of the load-cell device used, the results may not apply to other populations, and only acute responses were measured.
paper.practicalImplications: Choose hip position deliberately: NHE90 gave more knee flexion torque with less hamstring EMG, which may suit long-length eccentric loading and selective ST activation, while NHE0 gave more EMG, especially BFLH near full extension. Unilateral and bilateral versions gave similar peak torque and EMG at matched load, so single-leg work is a reasonable option. The study did not test whether unilateral work reduces side-to-side strength imbalance.
paper.athleteDev: Hip position changes the torque and EMG profile of the NHE. Use NHE90 when the goal is higher eccentric torque and selective ST activation at long hamstring lengths, and NHE0 when the goal is higher BFLH activity near full knee extension. Unilateral and bilateral NHE gave similar peak torque and EMG at matched load, so the choice between them did not change these measures.
paper.rtp: This study cannot inform return-to-sport decisions or hamstring injury risk. It measured acute torque and EMG in healthy amateur players and did not test injured athletes. The authors suggest, but do not test, that NHE90 may reduce injury risk.

records.sourceFile: Improving strength and power in trained athletes with 3     weeks of occlusion training.pdf

paper.citation: Cook CJ, Kilduff LP, Beaven CM. Improving Strength and Power in Trained Athletes With 3 Weeks of Occlusion Training. International Journal of Sports Physiology and Performance. 2014;9:166-172.
paper.abstract: Twenty male semiprofessional rugby union players each trained for two 3-week blocks, with and without intermittent 180 mmHg occlusion of the lower limbs, using 5 x 5 bench press, squat and pull-up at 70% 1RM. Occlusion produced greater gains in bench press, squat, sprint time, jump power and repeated-sprint maintenance, and larger acute salivary testosterone and cortisol responses, with the cortisol response attenuated over the block.
paper.tldr: In a small crossover study of 20 semiprofessional rugby players, adding lower-limb occlusion to moderate-load (70% 1RM) lifting gave larger strength, sprint and jump gains than the same training without occlusion over three weeks. The result comes from one squad over two short back-to-back blocks.
paper.methods: Twenty male semiprofessional rugby union players were split into two matched groups of 10 and completed two counterbalanced 3-week blocks of nine sessions, one with 180 mmHg intermittent occlusion on both thighs during exercise and one without. Sessions used 5 x 5 at 70% 1RM for squat, bench press and weighted pull-up. Outcomes were 1RM strength, countermovement-jump power, 40 m sprint time, repeated-sprint performance maintenance, and salivary testosterone and cortisol.
paper.findings: Occlusion gave larger improvements than control for bench press (5.4 vs 3.3 kg, P = .0044), squat (7.8 vs 4.3 kg, significant), best sprint time (-0.03 vs -0.01 s, P = .0162), countermovement-jump power (168 vs 68 W in the abstract, P = .0003) and repeated-sprint maintenance (0.74%, P = .0023). Acute salivary testosterone rose more after occlusion sessions, resting testosterone rose 8% across the occlusion block, and the acute cortisol response to occlusion was attenuated over the block. Acute testosterone response correlated with strength gains (r = .68 for squat).
paper.limitations: All 20 players came from one club in one preseason, and the two blocks ran consecutively within an 8-week preseason with no washout described, so carry-over between blocks is possible. Outcomes were strength, jump and sprint tests rather than muscle size or competition performance, and the hormone correlations do not show cause. The methods describe the players as semiprofessional but the practical applications call them elite, and the abstract reports changes in kg, s and W while the results report percentages. The text is an OCR scan with several garbled characters, including the squat P value.
paper.practicalImplications: For trained athletes in a short preseason block, adding intermittent lower-limb occlusion to 70% 1RM lifting may add strength, sprint and jump gains compared with the same lifting alone. The effect is shown for three weeks in one group of rugby players, so it should be trialed and monitored before it becomes a routine part of a program.
paper.athleteDev: Within a three-week preseason block, adding 180 mmHg lower-limb occlusion to moderate-load lifts produced larger gains in squat, bench press, sprint time and jump power than the same lifts without occlusion. The study shows the effect in trained semiprofessional rugby players only, over one short block.
paper.rtp: The authors suggest occlusion training may suit athletes returning from injury or who cannot tolerate high loads, but the study tested players in normal preseason training and did not include injured athletes or measure rehabilitation outcomes. It should not be used to set return-to-play loads or criteria.

records.sourceFile: Is it a slow day or a go day - The perceptions and applications of velocity-based training within elite strength and conditioning.pdf

paper.citation: Thompson SW, Olusoga P, Rogerson D, Ruddock A, Barnes A. "Is it a slow day or a go day?": The perceptions and applications of velocity-based training within elite strength and conditioning. International Journal of Sports Science & Coaching. 2023;18(4):1217-1228.
paper.abstract: Velocity-based training (VBT) is used in strength and conditioning for programming, testing and monitoring, but research procedures do not always reflect applied practice. This study interviewed 14 high-performance strength and conditioning coaches about their experiences of implementing VBT and analysed the interviews using reflexive thematic analysis. Three central themes emerged: technology, applications and reflections. Coaches perceived VBT as a beneficial and flexible tool, while noting drawbacks and challenges in some settings.
paper.tldr: Elite strength coaches value velocity-based training for objective load prescription, readiness tracking and driving intent, but they weigh it against cost, usability and the risk that chasing velocity harms technique. Their practice often differs from the research literature, which they seldom cite.
paper.methods: Semi-structured interviews, conducted remotely by Zoom, with 14 male high-performance strength and conditioning coaches recruited by purposive and opportunity sampling until data saturation. Transcripts were analysed using Braun and Clarke's six-phase reflexive thematic analysis with an inductive, realist approach, and the authors used Tracy's big-tent quality criteria, triangulation and member reflections to support credibility.
paper.findings: Coaches described buying technology on the basis of logistics, usability, data quality, cost and whether it suited performance or recruitment goals. They used velocity-based training mainly for key lifts, load-velocity profiling, velocity-loss thresholds, velocity zones and feedback to drive intent. They reported benefits such as individualised training, objective programme evaluation and readiness tracking, and drawbacks including chasing velocities, time demands, erroneous data and the risk of becoming an "iPad coach". Most coaches used simple methods rather than full load-velocity profiles, and few described relying on peer-reviewed research for their decisions.
paper.limitations: This is an interview study with 14 male coaches, so the themes reflect their perceptions and self-report rather than observed sessions or outcomes. The paper has no separate limitations section, but it states the principal investigator is a VBT researcher and practising coach, and the purposive and opportunity sample limits how far the findings generalise.
paper.practicalImplications: When choosing VBT technology, weigh usability, set-up time and cost alongside reliability, because coaches reported that ease of use and budget shaped purchases even though most saw data quality as essential. Velocity targets should be paired with technique cues, because coaches reported that chasing velocity can degrade lift technique, and load-velocity profiling should be kept to key exercises given its time cost.
paper.athleteDev: Coaches used velocity-based training to prescribe load and volume in key lifts, to autoregulate sets using velocity loss, and to drive intent with live feedback. Performance staff should set velocity targets with technique standards in place, and use simpler protocols such as velocity zones or velocity-loss cut-offs where time within sessions is limited.
paper.rtp: The study concerns elite strength and conditioning practice and does not address injury, rehabilitation or return to sport, so it cannot inform return-to-sport decisions.

records.sourceFile: Kinematics and kinetics of pick-up acceleration.pdf

paper.citation: Pryer ME, Cronin J, Neville J, Uthoff A. Kinematics and kinetics of pick-up acceleration. International Journal of Sports Science & Coaching. 2025:1-9.
paper.abstract: Narrative review that defines pickup acceleration (maximal acceleration from a submaximal, non-static entry) and proposes a step-analysis framework. It discusses the kinematics, kinetics and technical demands of the pickup steps, summarizes normative data, and outlines practical applications and future research directions.
paper.tldr: Accelerating from a moving start is a distinct motor quality that is under-studied. Most of the evidence comes from walking-entry studies with small samples, and jogging-entry data are largely missing.
paper.methods: Narrative review. The authors define pickup acceleration, name the steps of the transition (approach steps -2 and -1, transition step 0, pickup steps 1 and 2), and summarize kinematic and kinetic findings from gait-transition and sprint studies. No database search strategy is described.
paper.findings: The transition step shows the largest step-to-step velocity change (up to about 30 percent from walking), with accelerations of 2.62 to 3.63 m/s2. Vertical ground reaction force in pickup step 1 averages 174.93 percent of body weight, a 34 percent increase from the transition step. Kinetics for a jogging entry are described as largely unstudied, and the authors' own testing (Figure 1) showed athlete rankings for maximal acceleration changing between a static start and 1.5 or 3.0 m/s entries.
paper.limitations: Several cited studies had athletes hold a steady pace before accelerating to a controlled submaximal speed, so maximal acceleration may not have been measured. Normative data come from small groups, entry velocities differ across studies, and the authors call for more video and force-plate work before the step variables can be relied on.
paper.practicalImplications: Sprint drills for team sport athletes should be matched to the entry speed the athlete actually uses. The review suggests watching trunk lean and lower-body flexion in walking entries, recovery mechanics and stretch-shortening cycle use in jogging entries, and including lower-body range of motion work. These are the review's suggestions and have not been tested as a program.
paper.athleteDev: Test and train pickup acceleration as its own quality, because an athlete's rank for a static start can differ from their rank at a 1.5 or 3.0 m/s entry. Use the step framework to look for excessive braking and collapse in the approach steps and weak propulsion at the transition step.
paper.rtp: The review does not address return to sport or injury outcomes. It mentions tracking pickup mechanics as a possible way to judge readiness after injury, but gives no data, so it cannot be used to set return-to-play criteria.
